svg.title: Seven ways to detect a microplastic, one shared parts bin
svg.desc: Network diagram showing seven documented MPx detection methods and the recommended two-stage Path B concept, each traced across six shared design parameters from sampling interface to result communication, with shared design choices shown as converging nodes.
svg.text: Seven ways to detect a microplastic,
Every documented detection method — from a $10 phone clip to a patent-pending flow cell — reduces to
the same six design decisions. Read down a column to see the live design space at each stage; read
left to right to trace one method's specific choices; where lines converge on one box, two or more
methods made the identical call. The rust path is not a method in the literature — it's Path B, the
two-stage concept the team's morphological matrix synthesised by recombining an existing screen with

Each numbered circle is one documented method [1]–[7] entering the chain at P1. Tinted boxes are shared by ≥2 methods or by Path B. Dashed grey boxes mark a parameter the source material never specified — an open question, not a zero.
The solid rust line is TEMPT's own cheap, always-on turbidity screen, unchanged — it just keeps watching. The dashed
rust line is the accurate but slower fluorescence check from methods 1 and 3. Both report through one shared
microcontroller; the dashed line alone is wired to interrupt the phone app, so the expensive step only ever runs when
P2/P3/P4 converge hardest. Three methods independently landed on UV/blue fluorescence + a camera + YOLO (methods 1, 2, 3 overlap pairwise here) —
the field's default answer to “how do you see a microplastic,” and also exactly the expensive half of Path B's confirm stage.
P5/P6 are the most standardised. Smartphone-onboard compute and a phone-app readout cover four of the seven methods — the part of the product least
P1 is the most fragmented. Four genuinely different sampling interfaces, each tied to a different method family, with methods 2 and 7 undocumented
entirely — sampling is where the field has the least consensus, and where Path B's own choice (reusing [4]'s dip probe) is a real design decision.
Methods 5, 6 and 7 are the odd ones out. All three are patent or single-paper sources with 2–4 undocumented parameters, consistent with their “?
unknown” gates in the weighted ranking table — not new information.
Built from MPx's own CED Module 8 morphological matrix (MPx_Detection_Ranking_Morphological_Matrix.docx) and the 15-method sourced comparison
(MPx_Detection_Methods_Comparison.docx). Method numbering [1]–[15] matches those two documents exactly.
